sweep_summary: Amharic is not in the catalog. Of the four Glottolog title hits, two (Kapeliuk 2001 and its duplicate under the editor Zaborski) are a misspelled 'suprasentential constructions' paper on the discourse linker -mm - not about stress (verified from archive.org search-inside snippets of the printed volume). Downing 2010 'Accent in African languages' is paywalled at De Gruyter, but its open 2004 ZASPiL predecessor was fetched sources and read: a second-hand paragraph (from Leslau 1995, Richter 1987, Cowley et al. 1976) giving penultimate stress as the general tendency, initial stress in some trisyllables, stress on vowels before geminates and on roots over affixes, and pre-copula phrasal stress. Wedekind & Wedekind 1994 (ICES 11 proceedings, pp. 749-764; SIL bibliography subject 'Stress') is the one relevant item not obtainable - no digital copy exists on any open index reachable here; high priority for library acquisition. Best first-hand statement read: Mullen 1986 rule (41) p. 164 (quantity-sensitive: rightmost heavy non-final syllable, else leftmost; final consonants extrametrical), corroborated acoustically for its uncontested parts by Sande, Barzilai & Oakley 2019; older grammars (Armbruster 1908, Leslau 1995, Hayward & Hayward 1992, Hudson 1997) call stress weak/near-even with unstressed final syllables. New files (downing2004 pdf+txt, ia_fts/) and logged in there. Google Books API quota exceeded; HathiTrust, sil.org, Bing and DuckDuckGo blocked this client, so the Wedekind hunt relied on Crossref/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/archive.org/OpenLibrary only.

new_statements.quote: [Leslau 1995:44] 21. ACCENT 21.1. In general Amharic has an almost even distribution of stress on each syllable. It is safe to state that the last syllable is not stressed: thus, ሥጋ səga 'flesh' (and not səga [with final accent mark]); ወምበር wämbär 'chair' [...]. Note, however, that while in ተማሪ the stressed syllable is tämari 'student', in the combination ተማሪ ነው the stressed syllable is tämari näw 'he is a student'. In bisyllabic nouns the stress is on the 1st syllable [...]. In trisyllabic nouns the stress seems to vary [...]. [p.45] In quadrisyllabic nouns the stress is on the penultimate syllable [...]. The syllable preceding a geminated syllable is likely to be stressed: thus, ፈለገ fällägä, ፈላለገ fälallägä, ይፈልጋል yəfälləgal [...] || [Hayward & Hayward 1992:51] Stress is weak, and its position is variable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the reference grammar: stress is weak and nearly evenly distributed; the word-final syllable is not stressed; disyllabic nouns are stressed on the first syllable, quadrisyllabic nouns on the penult, trisyllables vary; a syllable immediately preceding a geminate tends to carry stress; position can shift in phrasal context (before the copula näw). The wider literature is contradictory: Alemayehu Haile 1987 (penult in verbs, antepenult in nouns), Mullen 1986 (rightmost non-final heavy syllable, else initial), Sande & Hedding 2017 (left-aligned trochees, geminate-closed syllables attract stress), versus Ullendorff 1955, Hayward & Hayward 1992 and the instrumental/perceptual studies of Kellogg & Barnes 2026 and Kellogg & Bayu 2026, which find no word-level stress (only Accentual-Phrase edge marking).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Leslau says nothing recoverable; Armbruster 1908:36 reports 'often a marked secondary accent' before and after a doubled consonant, 'sometimes almost equal to the principal accent'; Sande & Hedding posit alternating (odd-syllable) rhythmic stresses and multiple stresses on geminate-closed syllables; Voigt 2020 notes Hartmann 1980 distinguishes main and secondary tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Leslau: trisyllabic nouns vary (samuna 'soap' vs aräng‑ade 'green'); stress moves in phrases (tämari vs tämari näw). Mullen 1986:164-166: 'numerous lexical exceptions'; geminate-final suffixes such as plural -očč do not shift stress; person suffixes extrametrical; enclitics pull stress rightward. Hudson 1997: plural suffix may be stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Leslau's and Mullen's generalizations concern citation forms; Leslau and Cowley et al. 1976 both note heavier stress immediately before the copula näw, i.e. phrase-conditioned. Kellogg & Barnes (2026; in press ACAL 55), using focus-controlled carrier sentences with Addis Ababa speakers, find only word(AP)-initial strengthening and an AP-final H boundary tone and 'no acoustic evidence in support of prior descriptions of Amharic stress'; Kellogg & Bayu 2026 find Amharic listeners stress-'deaf'. Sande et al. 2019 (isolated words) find intensity higher on initial and geminate-closed syllables. Ullendorff 1955:197: in Ethio-Semitic 'the sentence accent predominates over such stress as might be apportioned to the individual word'.
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level amha1245. Leslau 1995 and Cowley et al. 1976 describe standard (Shewa/Addis Ababa) Amharic; Hayward & Hayward 1992's speaker is from Gondar ('extremely close to the Addis Ababa standard'); Kellogg & Barnes 2026 and Kaech 2022 explicitly study Addis Ababa Amharic; Mullen 1986 and Sande et al. work with diaspora native speakers. Divergent dialects (Gojjam, Mänz, Wällo) are not covered by any stress statement found.

new_statements.quote: (41) Amharic stress a. Stress falls on a heavy final syllable only i[n] bisyllabic words when the first syllable is light. b. Otherwise, the final syllable is skipped and [t]he rightmost heavy syllable is stressed. c. In the absence of any heavy syllable, the leftmost [of] a string of light syllables is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Mullen, Dana S. 1986. Issues in the morphology and phonology of Amharic: the lexical generation of pronominal clitics. PhD diss., University of Ottawa (hdl:10393/5402), §3.4 'Stress Assignment', rule (41), p. 164
new_statements.locator: printed p. 164 (PDF p. 173); on-disk scanned file lines 268-280
new_statements.reading: The only explicit first-hand placement rule read in this sweep: quantity-sensitive, right-edge oriented with final-consonant extrametricality (final CVC counts light) - rightmost heavy non-final syllable is stressed, a final heavy syllable only in L-H disyllables, and the leftmost syllable when all syllables are light; heavy = CVC (word-internal) or CVV, i.e. vowels before geminates are stressed. Quote is from a 200-dpi scanned with three bracketed letter restorations; its wording is independently confirmed by Sande, Barzilai & Oakley 2019: 3802-3803. Every other first-hand source read (Armbruster 1908, Leslau 1995, Hayward & Hayward 1992, Hudson 1997) stresses that stress is weak/near-even and final syllables are unstressed; Sande et al. 2019 confirm acoustically the points on which Mullen and Sande & Hedding agree but find neither analysis complete. Language is not in the catalog, so nothing is superseded.

sources.note: Quantity-sensitive, right-to-left with final-consonant extrametricality: rightmost heavy non-final syllable; final heavy syllable stressed only in L-H disyllables; otherwise leftmost syllable. Prefaced (p. 163) by 'as the linguistic commentators all agree, stress tends to be weak' and Cohen's 'Il est pratiquement impossible de désigner les syllabes accentuées'; notes lexical exceptions and unstressed plural -occ.

sources.citation: Armbruster, C. H. 1908. Initia Amharica: an introduction to spoken Amharic. Part I: Grammar. Cambridge: CUP. §8 'Accent', pp. 35-38.
sources.note: p.36: 'The stress accent in Amharic is in general much less marked than in English. Amharic speech, like French, runs with an almost even distribution of stress on each syllable... it is a matter of difficulty in many cases to detect where the principal accent of a particular word lies'; marked secondary accent before/after doubled consonants; perfect verb accented on the syllable preceding the doubled radical (gábba, láqqama); accent hardly ever on final i/u; enclitics throw accent back onto the preceding word's last syllable. Marks accent on every word throughout.

sources.citation: Kellogg, Jackson & Jonathan Barnes. 2026. Phrase-level prominence in Amharic in broad and narrow focus. Speech Prosody 2026 (Philadelphia), 118-122. doi:10.21437/speechprosody.2026-24.
sources.note: Treats Amharic as an 'edge-prominence' language (like French/Korean) 'including a purported lack of word-level stress' with H boundary tones at the right edge of a word-sized Accentual Phrase; 16 Addis Ababa speakers; focus marked by post-focal compression and edge strengthening; no word-stress placement rule.

sources.citation: Kellogg, Jackson & Melaku Bayu. 2026. Evaluating stress 'deafness' in Amharic vs. English speakers. Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 11(1): 6081. doi:10.3765/plsa.v11i1.6081.

sources.citation: Voigt, Rainer. 2020. On syllable weight in Amharic. Aethiopica 22 (2019): 236-245. doi:10.15460/aethiopica.22.0.1282.
sources.note: §1 'Stress in Amharic' surveys Armbruster 1908-20, Guidi 1924, Abraham 1942, Hartmann 1980, Leslau 1995, Klingenheben 1966 ('oscillation of the stress'): 'In general, the long vowels and the vowel before double consonants are stressed' (Armbruster's marking); jussive initial stress; 'the weak prominence of the stress is often commented upon'; quotes Cohen 1936:63 'On n'y peut noter aucun accent d'intensité ou de hauteur notable à des places déterminées'; §2 criticises Sande & Hedding 2017's data.

sources.citation: Sande, Hannah, Maya Barzilai & Madeleine Oakley. 2019. Acoustic correlates of stress in Amharic: implications for phonological analyses. Proceedings of ICPhS 2019 (Melbourne), 3802-3806.
sources.quote: The results show that intensity, measured here as rms, is the primary cue to stress in Amharic. Neither vowel duration nor pitch were significant predictors for stress in these data. ... We have also shown that neither extant phonological analysis of Amharic stress adequately accounts for the full range of data, and suggest that future phonological analyses of word-stress in Amharic consider at least three levels of stressedness.
sources.note: Instrumental (3 speakers, isolated words): intensity (rms), not duration or F0, correlates with syllables predicted stressed by Mullen 1986 and Sande & Hedding 2017 (initial syllable by default; syllables closed by geminates); neither analysis accounts for all data; suggests 'what we are calling stress in Amharic is in fact a combination of competing pressures for prominence' (word-initial and heavy syllables). Summarizes Leslau 1995, Hudson 1997, Armbruster, Alemayehu 1987, Mullen 1986.

sources.citation: Sande, Hannah & Andrew Hedding. 2014. Geminates and weight in Amharic. LSA Annual Meeting Extended Abstracts. doi:10.3765/exabs.v0i0.2373 (precursor of Sande & Hedding 2017, 'Syllable weight in Amharic', CILT 338: 69-82).
sources.note: 'The default stress pattern in Amharic involves binary, trochaic feet aligned to the left edge of a word... The initial syllable is stressed, as is every odd syllable. The final syllable is never stressed... Syllables closed by a geminate consonant attract stress' (other codas do not). Voigt 2020 shows many of their Amharic example forms are erroneous.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2004. What African languages tell us about accent typology. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 37: 101-136. (open-access predecessor of Downing 2010; fetched sources in this sweep)
sources.quote: in Amharic, a major language of Ethiopia and the most widely spoken Southern Semitic language, stress placement is described in terms of the following tendencies (Leslau 1995; Richter 1987). In general, the penultimate syllable is stressed (arängwáde 'green'). However, in three-syllable words, the first syllable is often stressed rather than the penult if its vowel is more sonorous than the penult vowel (sámuna 'soap'). Vowels preceding geminate consonants are also likely to be stressed (amäs´äggänä 'he thanked'). And stress is also more likely to fall on root vowels than affixal vowels.
sources.note: Survey (second-hand, citing Leslau 1995 and Richter 1987 Lehrbuch): penultimate stress as the general tendency, with initial stress in trisyllables when the initial vowel is more sonorous, stress on the vowel before a geminate, root vowels over affix vowels; adds (from Cowley et al. 1976) that the vowel before the copula näw is usually stressed (tämarí näw), and that 'these authors all suggest that the main correlates of stress are vowel quality and syllable duration, not pitch and loudness, which might be the reason the position of stress-accent is hard to determine'; concludes that 'stress…

sources.quote: Stress is not prominent in Amharic, though main stress of words is typically audible on stems rather than affixes (though the plural suffix may be stressed), but more so on closed rather than open syllables. There is, however, little research on this topic.
sources.note: 'Stress is not prominent in Amharic, though main stress of words is typically audible on stems rather than affixes (though the plural suffix may be stressed), but more so on closed rather than open syllables. There is, however, little research on this topic.'
